passage: Pallavi, you asked why grown-ups fight. Let me tell you about me as a girl of nine. Every night my parents' voices rose behind their door, and I was sure it was my doing, because of my poor maths marks and the socks I left on the floor. I began folding my clothes each night and studying until my eyes burned, trying to be better. One evening I finally asked Amma, "Are you fighting because of me?" She hugged me hard. "Never. That is between your father and me, and nothing you do could cause it." I cried, but my shoulders felt lighter. Children think everything is theirs to fix, Pallavi. If you wonder, ask. -- Himani

qa.q: What did Himani begin doing each night at the age of nine?
qa.a: She began folding her clothes each night and studying until her eyes burned.

qa.q: Why did Himani ask Amma if the fighting was because of her?
qa.a: She believed it might be her fault because of her maths marks and untidy socks, and she wanted to hear the truth.

qa.q: What should a parent say when a child wonders if the fighting is their fault?
qa.a: A parent should say clearly that it is between the adults and nothing the child does could cause it, as Amma told Himani.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel on hearing this story?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel reassured that another child once had the same worry, and that it is alright to ask; Himani ends by telling Pallavi to ask if there is a wondering.

grounding: An elder recalls blaming herself for her parents' fighting until her mother told her plainly it was not her doing.

passage: In the art room, Amandeep tore the corner off his drawing and shoved his chair back so hard it screeched. Jatin Sir looked up from his desk. "I'm furious with both of them," Amandeep blurted out. "They are wrecking our home." His fists were shaking. Jatin Sir did not tell him to calm down. He slid a fresh sheet and a thick black marker across the desk. "Draw how it feels." Amandeep scribbled hard until the paper nearly tore. Then his hand slowed. "Underneath, I'm just sad," he said, and his voice cracked. Jatin Sir said he could tell the school counsellor too, and his mother, when he was ready.

qa.q: What did Amandeep tear in the art room?
qa.a: He tore the corner off his drawing.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's remark "Underneath, I'm just sad" suggest about his anger?
qa.a: It suggests the anger was covering sadness about his parents, which came out once he began drawing his feelings.

qa.q: What helpful outlets did Jatin Sir offer for the anger?
qa.a: He gave him a fresh sheet and a marker to draw how it felt and suggested telling the school counsellor and his mother when ready.

qa.q: How might Jatin Sir see Amandeep's outburst?
qa.a: He seems to see it as a boy's pain rather than bad behaviour, since he did not tell him to calm down but gave him a way to express it.

grounding: A child angry at both parents in a school setting says it in words and drawing and finds the sadness underneath.

passage: I'm Chaitanya, Pradeep's desk partner. On Monday he was very quiet. At lunch he kept turning his spoon over and said both his parents say awful things about each other to him, and each one wants him to carry messages. "I love both," he said. I did not know what to say, so I just sat there. He looked at his hands. Later I saw him in the corridor telling the class teacher, "I don't want to stand between them." His voice was steady when he said it, but I can't tell how he really felt. I only know he looked a little lighter afterwards.

qa.q: Who did Pradeep tell that he did not want to stand between them?
qa.a: He told the class teacher in the corridor.

qa.q: How can you tell Pradeep felt torn between his parents?
qa.a: He kept turning his spoon over, said both parents say awful things about each other, and said he loves both.

qa.q: What could Pradeep say to each parent to protect himself?
qa.a: He can tell them kindly that he loves both of them and does not want to carry messages or stand between them.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt listening to Pradeep at lunch?
qa.a: Chaitanya did not know what to say, so Chaitanya probably felt unsure, wanted to help without knowing how, and stayed beside Pradeep instead.

grounding: A classmate observes a child who loves both parents and says he does not want to be in the middle.

passage: Sunday: Lakshmi set four plates on the table out of habit, then stared at the extra one. Her mother Sangeeta quietly took it away, and Lakshmi cried in the bathroom with the tap running. Wednesday: In class a maths sum blurred and her eyes filled for no reason she could name. She bent her head and let the tears fall on her notebook. Saturday: She still went to her swimming class, because the routine was hers to keep. Afterwards she told Sangeeta, "I miss how it was." "I know," Sangeeta said. "Me too, in a way. We do not have to be okay yet." They shared an ice cream and let themselves be sad.

qa.q: How many plates did Lakshmi set on Sunday?
qa.a: She set four plates on the table.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi's eyes fill during the maths sum on Wednesday?
qa.a: The passage gives no exact reason, but her plate habit and her later words "I miss how it was" suggest she was grieving the old family.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi cope during that week?
qa.a: She kept her swimming routine, let herself cry, and talked honestly to her mother about missing how it was.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta be feeling when she says "Me too, in a way"?
qa.a: She probably misses the old family too and is sad as well, but she stays gentle and lets Lakshmi know there is no hurry to be okay. 🤍

grounding: A child grieves the old family over several days, keeps routines and talks honestly with her mother.

passage: Tomas had a plan, written in green pen on a card: invite both parents to the same football match and sit them together. The stadium in Valencia was loud and sunny. His mum arrived first, then his dad, and they sat with one empty seat between them, polite as strangers. Tomas watched them instead of the game. On the tram home, his older brother Mateo said, "You can't fix it, you know. It's not your job." Tomas stared out the window. "I know," he said at last, "but I hoped." Mateo put an arm around him. The next Saturday Tomas went to a match with his dad and just enjoyed the goals.

qa.q: What did Tomas write his plan on?
qa.a: He wrote it in green pen on a card.

qa.q: What did Tomas hope would happen when he invited both parents to the match?
qa.a: He was hoping they would sit together and get back together, which is why he watched them instead of the game.

qa.q: What might help Tomas as he slowly accepts things?
qa.a: He can enjoy time with each parent separately, as he did with his dad at the next match, and talk with Mateo about his hope.

qa.q: How might Mateo see Tomas's plan?
qa.a: Mateo sees that fixing it is not Tomas's job and says so gently, then comforts him with an arm around him, so he seems kind rather than harsh.

grounding: A child hopes to reunite his parents through a plan, learns he cannot fix it, and accepts it slowly.

passage: Gurleen waited until the tractor noise faded from the lane and then sat on the charpai beside her son Nilesh. "Beta, your father and I will not live in the same house any more," she said. Nilesh's chin trembled. "It is nothing you did. We both love you, and that will not change." She said nothing against his father, though the words sat in her throat. Tomorrow he would still go to school, and on Sunday they would still make parathas. When Nilesh whispered, "Can I ask you things later?" she said yes. She did not ask him to carry a message to his father or to keep her secrets.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen sit when she told Nilesh about the separation?
qa.a: She sat on the charpai beside him.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say nothing against Nilesh's father even though the words sat in her throat?
qa.a: She wanted Nilesh to feel secure and not caught in the middle, so she kept her own hurt to herself.

qa.q: What routines did Gurleen point to in order to steady Nilesh?
qa.a: She reminded him he would still go to school and that on Sunday they would still make parathas.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt as his mother spoke?
qa.a: His chin trembled, so he was probably sad and frightened, and her calm words and promises about routines may have given him some steadiness.

grounding: A parent explains the split calmly, says it is not the child's fault, keeps routines and avoids using him as a messenger.

passage: The night the moving boxes appeared in the hallway, Lavanya could not sleep. She crept to the living room, where Nani Sarika sat rolling cotton wicks for the evening lamp. Nani opened her arms without a question, and Lavanya pressed her face into the soft cotton of her sari. "The house may change," Nani said, "but my love for you will not." Lavanya felt her breathing slow. Then she said honestly, "I'm scared, and I'm a bit angry too." Nani nodded. "Both are allowed. Tell me more." They stayed like that until the wicks were finished and Lavanya's eyes grew heavy.

qa.q: What was Nani Sarika doing when Lavanya came to the living room?
qa.a: She was rolling cotton wicks for the evening lamp.

qa.q: What did Lavanya admit she was feeling when she spoke to Nani?
qa.a: She said she was scared and also a bit angry.

qa.q: How did Nani make it easy for Lavanya to speak honestly?
qa.a: She opened her arms without any question, promised her love would not change, and said both feelings were allowed.

qa.q: What might Nani Sarika be feeling while she holds Lavanya?
qa.a: Nani is probably concerned for Lavanya and wants to be steady for her, and her nod and invitation to say more show she is ready to listen. 🤍

grounding: A steady grandmother comforts a child during a household change and the child speaks honestly.

passage: Ramesh's birthday get-together was set for Sunday, and everyone kept asking why his father would not be there. He mumbled that Papa was travelling. His stomach twisted; he had told nobody about the separation, and he felt ashamed, as if something were wrong with his family. On Saturday rain cancelled cricket, and the boys crowded onto the verandah, noisy and curious. Ramesh looked at Yamini, who had been his friend since Class 2 and never spread stories. He took a breath. "My parents live in separate homes now. Please don't tell anyone yet." Yamini nodded. "Thanks for telling me. Some kids in my building have the same." Ramesh felt a little lighter.

qa.q: How long had Yamini been Ramesh's friend?
qa.a: Yamini had been his friend since Class 2.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh say Papa was travelling?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and did not want his friends to know about the separation.

qa.q: What was wise about how Ramesh chose who to tell?
qa.a: He chose one trusted friend who never spread stories, and asked Yamini to keep it private.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Ramesh telling her?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt trusted and wanted to comfort him, as her thanks and her remark about other kids in her building show.

grounding: A child ashamed of his parents' separation hides it, then confides in one trusted friend.

passage: At her grandfather's house in the small town, Himani's mother Pallavi laid out a new bicycle helmet and a box of sweets. "All this is for my best girl," Pallavi said. "Wouldn't you rather live with me? Papa can't give you things like this." The gifts were shiny and Himani wanted them. But the words made her stomach knot. She fiddled with a sweet wrapper. "Mummy, I love you and Papa both," she said softly. "I don't want to choose. Can we just look at the helmet together?" Pallavi went quiet, her eyes wet. Himani felt sad for her but did not change what she had said. That night she told her aunt about it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi lay out for Himani?
qa.a: She laid out a new bicycle helmet and a box of sweets.

qa.q: Why did the words make Himani's stomach knot even though she wanted the gifts?
qa.a: She felt she was being asked to pick one parent in return for presents, and that felt wrong.

qa.q: What did Himani say that kept her from being treated as a prize?
qa.a: She said she loves both parents and does not want to choose.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Himani refuses to choose?
qa.a: Pallavi went quiet with wet eyes, so she may feel hurt and afraid of losing Himani, though that does not make it right to use gifts.

grounding: A child is offered gifts and hints to choose one parent and calmly says she loves both.

passage: Three weeks after Papa moved out, Rajni noticed the flat sounded different. No slammed doors, no stiff silence at dinner. She did her homework at the dining table while her mother hummed in the kitchen. Her shoulders dropped, and then came a hot prickle of guilt: was she a bad daughter for feeling better? At school she asked her friend Vishal, "Is it weird that I miss him and I also feel calm?" Vishal shrugged. "My cousin said the same thing." Rajni let out a shaky laugh. Both were true. She could miss Papa and still enjoy the quiet. That evening she called him and told him about her spelling test.

qa.q: What did Rajni do at the dining table while her mother hummed in the kitchen?
qa.a: She did her homework.

qa.q: Why did Rajni feel guilty about feeling calm?
qa.a: She wondered whether feeling better after her father left made her a bad daughter, because she also missed him.

qa.q: What could Rajni do about feeling both relief and sadness?
qa.a: She can accept that both feelings are true and keep her bond with her father, as she did by calling him.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Rajni's mixed feelings?
qa.a: Vishal seems to treat them as ordinary, since Vishal shrugged and said a cousin had said the same thing.

grounding: A child feels relief after a separation, then guilt, and accepts that both feelings are true.
